  diversity indices. *Assessing Writing* 47, 100505.
  doi:10.1016/j.asw.2020.100505

## Sensory cues, stratified vocabulary and sentence-length dynamics

Introduced in v0.8.0. These deterministic descriptors support passage review;
they do not estimate literary quality or a reader's experienced immersion.

- `sensory_density = 1000 * sensory_count / token_count`, using the selected
  language's combined sensory regular expression on prose. The lexicons cover
  auditory, visual, haptic/thermal and olfactory/gustatory cues in seven languages.
  `immersion_ratio = sensory_density / filter_density`; a zero filter density
  returns `null`, not an infinite or ideal score. Showing-report means use the
  comparable chapters, omitting unavailable ratios.
- `verb_mattr` and `desc_mattr` apply MATTR to ordered, lowercased token subsets.
  Verb candidates match present/past morphology; descriptive candidates match
  adjective or nominal morphology with nominal exclusions. These are heuristic
  categories, not contextual POS tags. For a category sequence of length N and
  window w, MATTR is the mean of `unique(window) / w` over its N-w+1 windows.
  Fewer than w category tokens returns `null`. The implementation's default
  category window is defined by `DEFAULT_STRATIFIED_WINDOW` in `diversity.py`.
- For sentence token lengths L, `sentence_cv = population_stddev(L) / mean(L)`.
  `compute_rhythm_profile()` (`pacing.py`) also computes `asl_iqr`, three-bucket
  Shannon entropy (`length_entropy`, `normalized_entropy`), and finite-sample
  Goh–Barabási `burstiness()` (Kim & Jo 2016):
  $B_n = \frac{\sqrt{n}(r - 1)}{(\sqrt{n} - 2)r + \sqrt{n}}$ clamped to $[-1, 1]$,
  using sample SD $s$ and $r = s / \bar{x}$. The direct API requires finite
  nonnegative observations and returns `null` for fewer than two observations
  or an all-zero sample. The implementation scales a positive sample by its
  maximum before forming the ratio to keep squared deviations in range.
  Rolling sentence length uses w=N for fewer than six sentences, otherwise
  `w=min(15,max(3,N//3))`. Sliding means are rounded to one decimal and, when
  longer than twelve points, averaged into twelve contiguous index bins.
  `pacing_curve` retains those means; `pacing_sparkline` rescales each chapter's
  own minimum and maximum to eight display levels. A constant curve uses one
  middle level. Empty sentence input has an empty curve and sparkline; its
  current numeric CV sentinel is zero and must not be read as measured regularity.

<a id="revision-time-series-and-session-deltas-unreleased"></a>
<a id="revision-time-series-and-session-deltas"></a>

## Revision time-series and session deltas

- On every saved edit in `ManuscriptStore.save()` (`manuscript_editing.py`), both
  the pre-edit baseline revision (if not yet recorded) and the resulting
  revision are stored in `manuscript_revisions` inside `recovery.sqlite3`.
- Each revision records deterministic `CorpusAnalyzer` measurements: `words`
  (`clean_words`), `sentences` (`total_sentences`), `asl` (when `sentences > 0`,
  else `null`), `asl_cv` (when `sentences > 0`, else `null`), `dialogue_ratio`
  (when `tokens > 0`, else `null`), `mattr` (when window-eligible, else `null`),
  and per-chapter `{num, title, words, asl, dialog_pct}` snapshots.
- `ManuscriptStore.delta(base_revision, target_revision)` subtracts the
  baseline from the target for comparable measurements. Count differences are
  integers. Decimal differences are rounded to the field's precision. An
  unavailable endpoint yields a `null` difference.
- A default comparison for the latest recorded revision considers the most
  recent 100 entries. It uses the earliest other entry at or before the target
  on the same UTC calendar day, or the preceding entry if none falls on that
  day. A current file outside the recorded history has no implicit baseline.
- When measurement rules or settings differ, Lixity remeasures verified
  retained text under the effective configuration. Automatic language selection
  uses the target to choose a common language. If a comparison cannot be
  established, `has_baseline` is `false` and `deltas` is `null`. The stored
  timeline remains available as recorded and gaps remain visible.

<a id="dramaturgical--structural-heuristics-unreleased"></a>
<a id="dramaturgical--structural-heuristics"></a>

## Dramaturgical & structural heuristics

- **Sticky sentences & glue-word density (`pacing.py`):** for each prose
  sentence with `N >= sticky_min_words` (default `8`) tokens, glue-word density
  is `glue_pct = 100 * glue_words / N`, where `glue_words` counts lowercased
  tokens present in the active language's `function_words` lexicon. A sentence
  is flagged sticky when `N >= sticky_min_words` and `glue_pct >= sticky_glue_pct`
  (default `45.0`, configurable in `CorpusConfig` on `(0, 100]`). Multiply the
  integer count by 100 before dividing so an intermediate rounding error
  cannot move an exact percentage below the inclusive cutoff. Corpus and
  chapter reports expose `sticky_sentences`, `sticky_sentence_pct`,
  `mean_glue_pct`, `sticky_available` (`false` when the language has no
  `function_words` lexicon, e.g. `generic`), and `sticky_items` (top 50 by
  descending `glue_pct`: `{chapter_num, scene_index, words, glue_words,
  glue_pct, preview}`).
- **Dialogue tag density (`dialogue.py`):** counts speech-attribution verbs
  matching curated per-language inventories (`en`, `de`, `fr`, `es`, `it`,
  `pt`, `nl`; `dialogue_tag_available = false` for `generic`). Per-chapter and
  corpus reports expose `dialogue_tags`,
  `dialogue_tag_pct = min(100.0, 100 * dialogue_tags / turns)` (when `turns > 0`),
  and `dialogue_tags_per_1000 = 1000 * dialogue_tags / words` (when `words > 0`).
- **Scene entry/exit hooks (`pacing.py`, `scenes.py`):** `classify_scene_hook`
  classifies the first (`entry_hook_type`) and last (`exit_hook_type`) non-empty
  prose sentence of each scene as `"dialogue"` (matches `dialogue_re` or begins
  with an opening quote/dash), `"question"` (ends with `?` ignoring trailing
  quotes/brackets), `"reflection"` (matches `filter_verbs_re` or curated
  cognitive/perception cue verbs), `"action"` (fallback for non-empty prose),
  or `"unknown"` (empty). Scenes also expose `exit_hook_score` (`0–3`) and
  `scenes.hook_distribution` (`{"entry": {...}, "exit": {...}}`).
- **POV chapter-absence gaps (`characters.py`, `scenes.py`):** when character
  profiles define `declared_pov_chapters`, `pov_chapters_map` attaches
  `pov_characters` to `scenes.items[]`, and `presence_report` computes per-figure
  `pov_gaps` (`{from_chapter, to_chapter, gap_chapters, missing_chapters}` for
  each contiguous gap between consecutive declared POV chapters),
  `pov_longest_gap`, `pov_leading_gap` (`first_pov - 1`), `pov_trailing_gap`
  (`total_chapters - last_pov`), and `pov_share` (`len(pov_chapters) / total_chapters`,
  rounded to 4 decimals), plus corpus-level `pov_summary`
  (`{declared_figures, pov_coverage_chapters, chapters_without_declared_pov}`).
- **Optional genre reference corridors (`corridors.py`):** `GENRE_CORRIDORS`
  (inspectable at runtime via `lixity.corridors.list_genre_corridors()`)
  defines descriptive orientation bands over `asl`, `dialogue_pct`,
  `staccato_pct`, and `avg_scene_words`:
  - `crime_thriller` (*Crime / Thriller*): `asl` `10.0–16.0`, `dialogue_pct` `25.0–50.0`, `staccato_pct` `15.0–35.0`, `avg_scene_words` `800.0–2200.0`
  - `literary` (*Literary Fiction*): `asl` `14.0–24.0`, `dialogue_pct` `15.0–40.0`, `staccato_pct` `8.0–25.0`, `avg_scene_words` `1200.0–3500.0`
  - `romance` (*Romance*): `asl` `11.0–18.0`, `dialogue_pct` `30.0–55.0`, `staccato_pct` `12.0–30.0`, `avg_scene_words` `1000.0–2800.0`
  - `speculative` (*Speculative / Sci-Fi / Fantasy*): `asl` `13.0–20.0`, `dialogue_pct` `20.0–45.0`, `staccato_pct` `10.0–28.0`, `avg_scene_words` `1200.0–3200.0`
  `evaluate_genre_corridor` sets `non_prescriptive: true` and
  reports each metric's `{observed, low, high, position}` where `position` is
  `"below"`, `"within"`, `"above"`, or `"unavailable"`.
- **Paragraph inline evidence layers (`paragraph_evidence.py`):** each
  paragraph's `evidence[idx]["layers"]` includes four additional deterministic
  annotation layers:
  - `sticky` (`kind: "sentence"`): character spans (`{start, end, count: 1, words}`)
    for sentences with `words >= config.sticky_min_words` and
    `glue_pct >= config.sticky_glue_pct`; returns `status: "unavailable"`,
    `reason: "language_unavailable"` when the language lacks `function_words`.
  - `dialogue_tag` (`kind: "pattern"`): character spans (`{start, end, count: 1}`)
    for speech-attribution verbs adjacent to dialogue quotes; returns
    `status: "unavailable"`, `reason: "language_unavailable"` when the language
    has no dialogue tag verb list.
  - `echo` (`kind: "word"`): character spans (`{start, end, count: 1}`) for
    words of length `>= 4` repeated `>= 2` times in the same paragraph. The
    function-word list excludes matching words where the profile provides one.
  - `indirect_speech` (`kind: "pattern"`): character spans for language-specific
    language-profile cues for reported speech or thought outside detected quotations.
- **Deep dialogue analytics (`dialogue.py`):** `dialogue_report().to_dict()`
  adds:
  - `voice_separation`: compares Spoken Dialogue against Narrative Prose via
    `{available, dialogue_words, narrative_words, dialogue_asl, narrative_asl,
    asl_delta, dialogue_question_excl_pct, narrative_question_excl_pct,
    cosine_similarity, separation_label}` where `separation_label` is
    `"unavailable"` when `dialogue_words == 0` or `narrative_words == 0`,
    `"distinct"` when `cosine_similarity < 0.45` or (`asl_delta` is available
    with `|asl_delta| >= 6.0` and `cosine_similarity < 0.65`), `"moderate"`
    when `cosine_similarity < 0.72`, and `"blended"` otherwise (fixed heuristic
    cutoffs, not calibrated probabilities).
  - `adverbial_tags` (int), `adverbial_tag_pct` (float), and
    `adverbial_tag_available` (bool) at corpus level and per `chapters[]` entry,
    counting speech-attribution tags accompanied by manner adverbs. The
    per-language regex patterns and non-manner exclusion sets
    (`_MANNER_ADVERB_PATTERNS`, `_NON_MANNER_ADVERBS` in `dialogue.py`) are
    curated language-profile implementation details (`en`, `de`, `fr`, `es`,
    `it`, `pt`, `nl`; unavailable for `generic`).
- **Within-scene changes (`scenes.py`):** `scene_report()` keeps `asl_shift`
  and `dialogue_shift` (`float | null`) and the `scene_dynamic` wire values
  `"accelerating"`, `"decelerating"`, `"dialogue_surge"`, `"steady"`, and
  `"insufficient_length"`. The interface describes the measured changes in
  words per sentence and percentage points. See the
  [method cards](#scene-evidence-and-dramaturgical-rehearsal) for the minimum
  sample and the count fields that support the displayed comparisons. The
  scene report also includes `filter_per_1000` and `sensory_per_1000`. In
  `scene_report()`, a word-bearing scene unit with `sentences == 0` reports
  `features.asl = null` (with target position `"unavailable"` and exclusion from
  group baselines), while `CorpusMetrics.asl` and `ChapterMetrics.asl` retain
  their numeric `0.0` schema-2 sentinel. When `_include_draft_evidence=True`,
  `source_sha256` (`scene_source_sha256` in dossier drafts) hashes the scene's
  normalized prose projection (`scene.text`), not raw manuscript bytes. Corpus-level
  `pacing_plateaus` lists `[{start_id, end_id, scene_count, mean_asl, reason}]`
  where `reason` is `"low_exit_hooks"` (`>= 3` consecutive scenes with
  `exit_hook_score <= 1`; `mean_asl` is `null` if no scene in the plateau has a
  measured `features.asl`) or `"flat_pacing"` (`>= 3` `"steady"` scenes of
  `>= 120` words with ASL spread `<= 1.5`).
- **Implicit scene breaks & lexical cohesion drops (`scenes.py`):** `scene_report()`
  exposes top-level `implicit_breaks`: `[{chapter, scene, paragraph_index,
  cue_type, cohesion_similarity, snippet}]`, where `paragraph_index` is 1-based
  within the chapter's prose paragraphs (scanning adjacent paragraphs inside the
  same explicit scene), `cohesion_similarity` is the Jaccard similarity of
  lowercase non-function/non-stopword tokens (`>= 3` characters) across adjacent
  2-paragraph windows inside the scene, and `cue_type` is `"time"`, `"place"`,
  `"character"`, `"cohesion_drop"` (when both windows have `>= 10` content words
  and `cohesion_similarity <= 0.05`), or `+`-joined combinations (e.g.
  `"time+cohesion_drop"`). An implicit `"character"` cue compares disjoint sets
  of recurring capitalized tokens (appearing in `>= 2` paragraphs of the chapter
  outside `_NON_NAME_CAPS` and German article predecessors, or configured
  character names; disabled for unconfigured German prose) between the previous
  paragraph and the opening 60 characters of the current paragraph — it is a
  surface token heuristic, not NER or narrative POV. Descriptive shift markers
  relate to the distinct
  scene-segmentation task studied by [Zehe et al. (2021)](https://aclanthology.org/2021.eacl-main.276/)
  and [Zehe et al. (2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.naacl-long.500/).
- **Character voice separation & interaction matrix (`dialogue.py`, `characters.py`):**
  `character_voice_profiles()` (and `presence_report()["character_voices"]`)
  computes `{min_turns: 3, narrator: {words, asl, question_excl_rate,
  function_word_share}, characters: [{name, status, turns, min_turns, words,
  dialogue_asl, question_excl_rate, function_word_share, narrator_asl_delta,
  narrator_question_excl_delta, narrator_function_word_delta}]}`. Rates and
  shares are percentages in `[0, 100]`, and deltas are `character - narrator`.
  Attribution uses deterministic single-speaker adjacent-window matching
  (ambiguous turns are skipped; below `min_turns = 3`, `status` is
  `"insufficient_turns"` with `null` metrics). Both `character_voice_profiles()`
  and `presence_report()` also expose `character_interactions`:
  `{pairs: [{a, b, turn_exchanges, co_chapters}], turn_dominance: [{name, turns,
  words, word_share, turn_share}]}`, where `turn_exchanges` counts adjacent
  attributed turns with different speakers (reset on unattributed turns and
  chapter boundaries) and `co_chapters` counts chapters where both characters
  are mentioned or speak. Motivated by character voice profiling in literary
  dialogue (Michel et al., EMNLP 2024).
- **Rhythm profile & sentence-length entropy (`pacing.py`):** `PacingReport` and
  `ChapterPacing` expose `rhythm_profile`: `{available, sentences, asl_cv,
  asl_iqr, length_entropy, normalized_entropy, bucket_shares}` with
  `bucket_shares: {short, medium, long}`. Short sentences have at most
  `short_sentence_max` words (default `6`). Medium sentences exceed that
  limit and have at most 20 words. Long sentences exceed both limits.
  `asl_cv = std / mean`,
  `asl_iqr = Q75 - Q25`, `length_entropy = -sum(p_b * log2(p_b))` in bits over
  non-empty buckets (max `log2(3) ≈ 1.585` bits), and
  `normalized_entropy = length_entropy / log2(3)`. When `sentences < 2`,
  `available: false` and all numeric metrics are `null`. Tracks sentence-length
  dispersion against narrative flattening (Li et al., 2026; CHR 2024/2025).
- **Indirect speech detection (`paragraph_evidence.py`, `dialogue.py`):**
  `paragraph_evidence.py` adds `layers["indirect_speech"]` (`kind: "pattern"`,
  `ParagraphCounts.indirect_speech`, `status: "available" | "unavailable"`,
  `reason: "language_unavailable"` for `generic`), and `DialogueReport` /
  `DialogueChapter` expose `indirect_speech`, `indirect_speech_per_1000`, and
  `indirect_speech_available`. Matches non-quoted reporting/reflection verbs
  followed by complementizers across all seven supported languages (`en`, `de`,
  `fr`, `es`, `it`, `pt`, `nl`) plus German third-person *Konjunktiv I* and
  reporting-verb-attributed *Konjunktiv II* speech forms (`_INDIRECT_SPEECH_PATTERNS`
  in `dialogue.py`, curated per-language implementation detail; GermAnProse,
  LaTeCH-CLfL 2026; CHR 2024/2025).
- **Enriched revision diff (`manuscript_editing.py`, `cli.py`, `mcp.py`):**
  `analyze_manuscript_snapshot()`, `ManuscriptStore.analyze_snapshot()`,
  `timeline()`, `delta()` (`schema_version: "lixity-timeline/1"`), and
  `compare_texts()` (`schema_version: "lixity-diff/1"`) include
  `length_entropy` (4 decimals), `sticky_pct` (2 decimals), and
  `indirect_speech_per_1000` (2 decimals) alongside `words`, `sentences`, `asl`,
  `asl_cv`, `dialogue_ratio`, `mattr`, `flags_count`, and `chapter_deltas`.
  Exposed via `lixity diff` and the read-only `revision_diff` MCP tool.

### Scene evidence and dramaturgical rehearsal

The scene panel keeps measured text in manuscript order and identifies each
claim using the [evidence ladder](LOCALIZATION.md#evidence-levels-for-analysis-claims).
An explicit divider defines a scene unit. In its absence, the panel identifies
the chapter used as the unit. Counts use the configured word regex and the
shared quotation projection. The method cards below state how to reproduce
the two tracks and their details.

| Level and measure | Formula and scope | Guard and interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| L0 · Quoted-word share | `100 × recognized quoted words / counted words` for the complete unit. The same token membership is used for `features.dialog_pct` and the block detail. | An empty denominator gives an unavailable share. Zero recognized words in a non-empty unit describes the output of the configured recognizer. The track has a fixed 0–100% scale. |
| L0 · Words per sentence | `counted sentence words / counted sentences`, the scene's `features.asl`. Both tracks follow manuscript order. | A zero sentence count in a word-bearing scene unit sets `features.asl` to `null` (target position `"unavailable"`, omitted from register baselines; `CorpusMetrics.asl` and `ChapterMetrics.asl` keep their numeric `0.0` schema-2 sentinel). The track uses a shared panel scale in words per sentence. The measurement describes text length. [Genette, Duration, pp. 86–88](https://utpdistribution.com/9780801410994/narrative-discourse/) |
| L1 · Within-scene change | Split the counted sentences at `floor(n / 2)` in manuscript order. Each half retains `words`, `sentences` and `quote_words` in `within_scene`. Changes are second minus first and are displayed to two decimal places in words per sentence (`asl_shift`) and percentage points (`dialogue_shift`). | A unit needs at least 120 words and two counted sentences. `within_scene_limits` reports the guard and the descriptive cutoffs for the compatibility class (2.5 words per sentence, 15 percentage points). The signed differences describe the two halves. Scene-level standard errors are separate from these descriptive half differences. |
| L2 · Quotation-block lengths | Count positive word lengths of the unioned recognized quotation ranges using the same word membership. `quote_blocks.short` counts lengths ≤ `short_max_words`, `long` counts lengths ≥ `long_min_words`, and `medium` counts lengths strictly between them. `words` totals the counted quoted words. | `quote_block_limits` reports the configured cutoffs, 12 and 80 words by default. `unresolved_ranges` counts unresolved ranges separately. Nested or overlapping recognized marks share a block. Any longer narrative or acoustic unit would need a separate annotation. [Genette, Duration, pp. 86–88](https://utpdistribution.com/9780801410994/narrative-discourse/) |
| L3 · Author intent | An authored card can place a question, delayed answer, turn, revelation or resolution against the text. The author supplies any voice note and effect hypothesis. The card sequence can be rehearsed independently of the measured text. | It is an explicit act of revision planning. **Who has the floor here?** is a reading question. The quote analysis supplies no speaker identity. [Bakhtin, Discourse in the Novel](https://utpress.utexas.edu/9780292715349/) |

For example, two units can each have 96 recognized quoted words among 192
counted words. With the default cutoffs, twelve 8-word blocks and one 96-word
block both produce 50% quoted words. Their L2 distributions differ. Reporting
clauses can interrupt a block, and a quotation can represent a letter or a
cited expression. Fictional elapsed time requires evidence about depicted
events. Questions about the relationship between voices require reading their
context. [Genette (1980), *Narrative Discourse*](https://utpdistribution.com/9780801410994/narrative-discourse/) ·
[Bakhtin (1981), *The Dialogic Imagination*](https://utpress.utexas.edu/9780292715349/)

The order of disclosure matters as a reading question. Fish considers
interpretation as it unfolds, Iser describes a shifting viewpoint, and Jauss
places expectations in the context of prior reading and history. For Lixity,
this motivates showing measures in manuscript order, and letting authors
revisit an intent after revision with the outcome already in mind. Displaying
counts, scope and cutoffs makes the construction of the observations visible.
[Fish (1970), *New Literary History* 2(1), 123–162](https://doi.org/10.2307/468593) ·
[Iser (1978), *The Act of Reading*](https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/2456/act-reading) ·
[Jauss (1970), *New Literary History* 2(1), 7–37](https://www.jstor.org/stable/468585) ·
[Drucker (2011), *Digital Humanities Quarterly* 5(1)](https://dhq-static.digitalhumanities.org/pdf/000091.pdf)

Structural-affect and narratological work motivates rehearsing different
orders of disclosure. Hoeken and van Vliet report suspense among readers who
knew the outcome of the story in their experiment. Gerrig's three experiments
recorded disruptions in verifying facts that readers already knew. These
findings remain L4 study evidence. The rehearsal provides an L3 author
hypothesis about the sequence. Reader effects and literary quality are outside
the scene measurements.
[Brewer & Lichtenstein (1982), *Journal of Pragmatics* 6(5–6), 473–486](https://doi.org/10.1016/0378-2166%2882%2990021-2) ·
[Sternberg (1990), *Poetics Today* 11(4), 901–948](https://www.jstor.org/stable/1773082) ·
[Sternberg (1992), *Poetics Today* 13(3), 463–541](https://www.jstor.org/stable/1772872) ·
[Gerrig (1989), *Journal of Memory and Language* 28(6), 633–648](https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-596X%2889%2990001-6) ·
[Hoeken & van Vliet (2000), *Poetics* 27(4), 277–286](https://research-portal.uu.nl/en/publications/suspense-curiosity-and-surprise-how-discourse-structure-influence/)

Modern computational work targets different tasks. CHIRON evaluates rich
character representations through tasks such as masked-character prediction.
The scene-segmentation studies define and evaluate annotated narrative
boundaries. Neither result validates these surface measurements as scene
detectors or speaker attribution. [Gurung & Lapata (2024)](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-emnlp.499/) ·
[Zehe et al. (2021)](https://aclanthology.org/2021.eacl-main.276/) ·
[Zehe et al. (2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.naacl-long.500/)

#### Exploratory author study proposal

Recruit 8–12 authors for a within-subject usability study. Use three synthetic
fixtures with predefined measurement changes, plus passages from chapter 26 of
*Effi Briest* and chapter 35 of *Pride and Prejudice*. Include an equal-share
pair with different block lengths, a signed within-scene change, and a fixture
with insufficient support or unresolved quotation marks. Freeze the baseline
scene panel at a named revision. Counterbalance condition order and passage
assignment across authors. Record prior familiarity with the public passages
and language proficiency. [Fontane, Project Gutenberg #5323](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5323) ·
[Austen, Project Gutenberg #1342](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1342)

| Question | Procedure and outcome |
| --- | --- |
| RQ1 · Locate a measured change | Compare the baseline scene panel with the two-track reading view on matched tasks. Record the first correctly identified passage or boundary, task time and number of text-specific revision questions. Synthetic fixtures supply exact target locations. For published passages, predefine permissible observations and record ambiguities. |
| RQ2 · Formulate a revision question | Compare the scene review task with and without the intent card, holding measured evidence constant. Two raters independently code think-aloud records for a specific passage, a stated intent, and a question the author can check. Record counts, agreement and Cohen's κ per binary criterion when estimable, before adjudicating disagreements. |
| RQ3 · Revisit an intent | After an assigned revision to a synthetic text, ask authors to find the held-over intent, explain its review state, and reopen the relevant passage. Compare previously reviewed and unreviewed states. Record recovery and interpretation accuracy, time and whether the author explicitly confirms after rereading. |

Preregister the materials, assignment, hypotheses, rubric, exclusions and
stopping rule before recruitment. Keep consent, recordings and identifiable
notes outside the repository. Report task completion, missing results and
within-author differences descriptively with the exact sample and limitations.
The outcomes are about using the interface. They exclude reader affect,
literary merit and prose quality. The existing nominal FDR estimates concern
manuscript diagnostics and do not calibrate study outcomes. Research on
foregrounding and engagement uses its own materials and observations.
[Miall & Kuiken (1994), *Poetics* 22(5), 389–407](https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-422X%2894%2900011-5) ·
[Busselle & Bilandzic (2009), *Media Psychology* 12(4)](https://doi.org/10.1080/15213260903287259)

## Manuscript evidence in dossier suggestions

The preview keeps the source and the reason for selection separately.
Character candidates come from configured names or capitalized names that
recur in separate paragraphs of a chapter. Place candidates come from a
configured list or a repeated capitalized expression near a spatial cue, with
at least one directional cue. The inferred place preview gives that
directional passage separately from the first counted name match. Scene
suggestions use explicit separators or the whole chapter and present the
measured opening and closing sentence. Implicit shift cues stay in scene
analysis.

Counts describe the matching rule. A name can refer to different people or
places, while a pronoun or description can refer to the same one. Literary
entity annotation and coreference are separate tasks. The current dossier
generator records the name evidence so authors can resolve such cases in
context. The cited datasets cover English literary text.
[Literary entities](https://aclanthology.org/N19-1220/) ·
[Coreference in English literature](https://aclanthology.org/2020.lrec-1.6/)

For examples and adjustable inference and report settings, see the
[manuscript dossier workflow](research/USAGE.md#manuscript-driven-dossier-drafts).

===============================================================================
## docs/STABILITY.md

Source: https://github.com/mfahsold/lixity/blob/main/docs/STABILITY.md

# Stability & known limitations

> Version line: this documentation describes source **v0.9.3** on the pre-1.0 **0.x** line.
> Historical 1.x/3.x tags predate the numbering reset; a larger number does not mean a newer release.

Use this page to judge what a result can support. Formula details live in
[METHODS.md](METHODS.md); machine-readable thresholds and availability policies
come from `lixity about --json`. This page keeps interpretation and integration
limits that a passing check cannot resolve. Statistical signals support human
review, not a prose grade.

## Scope of linguistic use

Lixity supports descriptive exploration of supplied prose. Its chapter baseline
is internal to that text; it is not a population norm. Comparisons across texts
need compatible preprocessing, segmentation, language resources and settings.
A difference in a measure does not establish an author's identity or intention,
a causal explanation, or a literary-quality ranking. Software tests establish
implementation behavior, not empirical validity for every genre or language.

## 1. Research findings (state of the art)

### Release verification and limits

The maintained suite checks English defaults, language resource-key coverage,
readability-coefficient dispatch and locale formatting. These are software
contracts, not empirical validation of linguistic accuracy across seven
languages. No language-wide accuracy percentage is established by this suite.

The 3D chapter view is exploratory: its dimensions are corpus-specific, signs
are fixed by convention, and per-axis thresholds are not simultaneous confidence
regions. Native rotation/zoom buttons and a chapter-score table provide keyboard and touch access to the displayed scores,
flag status and chapter navigation. Individual canvas points remain pointer-operated.
These targeted checks do not establish full assistive-technology coverage.
The same raw-score cutoff represents different multiples of the sample
standard deviation on axes with different spreads. The dashboard reports those
multiples to aid interpretation; this is not a calibrated significance test.
The relative threshold is withheld for numerically negligible axis spreads.

Engine tests use synthetic/public samples. Project adapters and optional local
servers have separate trust boundaries and need their own tests; core test
success is not a security certification for an arbitrary adapter.

<a id="grammatical-german-tense"></a>

### Grammatical tense

The optional local model path covers all seven supported analysis languages and
is a contextual grammatical measurement, not a
linguistic correctness guarantee. The standard installation uses incomplete
lexical patterns. In v0.7.6 German unknown adjectives ending in `-ten` can match
past cues. Version 0.7.7 removes that unrestricted German suffix rule and adds
selected forms such as `übt`; unlisted regular past forms such as `flatterten`
can now be missed. Listed forms and auxiliary/participle matches can still be
ambiguous: for example, `Ich habe gelben Stoff` can still produce a spurious
past cue from `habe gelben`. This changes counts and dependent results, so regenerate analyses and
review previous decisions. The default matcher skips some capitalized German
nominal forms after fused articles, such as `beim Lesen`. Other noun–verb
ambiguities still require context. Other languages retain their existing patterns. To use
the contextual path, explicitly select an installed model as described in
[Usage](USAGE.md#grammatical-tense).

The initial construction comparison used 40 newly written German sentences with
manually assigned verb-group tense/mood labels, available in
`tests/fixtures/german_verb_groups.json`. All systems used the same Lixity
composition rules. It is a development construction set, not an independent,
representative or held-out literary benchmark. Final matching-sentence counts:

| Installed parser | Fully matching cases / 40 |
| --- | --- |
| spaCy `de_core_news_md` 3.8.0 | 39 |
| spaCy `de_core_news_sm` 3.8.0 | 36 |
| ZDL `de_zdl_lg` 4.0.0 | 33 |
| Stanza 1.15.0, German HDT resources | 31 |

These numbers evaluate complete sentence label sequences on this set, not token
accuracy or editorial-warning precision. Stanza was compared through a temporary
UD adapter; the shipped runtime uses spaCy. The small model sometimes mistakes
modal/coordinate forms; the tested HDT models supplied incorrect mood features
for several subjunctives. This supports selecting `de_core_news_md` as the initial
CPU option, not declaring it universally superior. Model load/memory and
long-manuscript throughput were not established by the short construction score.
Reproduce the spaCy comparison from a development checkout with installed models:

```sh
python scripts/check_grammatical_tense.py de_core_news_sm de_core_news_md de_zdl_lg
```

The remaining md error is `Übe jeden Tag!`, tagged as indicative present rather
than imperative. In the separate existing public-domain *Effi Briest* excerpt,
the model correctly tags seven preterite predicates but misreads adjectival
`weiß` in `blau und weiß gestreiftes …` as a present verb. That is a real false
positive, not an accepted gold label. Ambiguous `sein` constructions may be
reported unresolved. Indirect/free indirect discourse and semantic narrative
time are not recognized automatically. Selecting `narration` only excludes spans
recognized by the configured quotation pattern, including its capture convention;
it must not be presented as reliable speaker attribution.

Future, subjunctive and unresolved groups stay inspectable rather than being
silently turned into past/present evidence. A zero count is the number of
resolved selected indicative groups, not proof that the paragraph contains no
verbs or tense changes. Model absence or failure is an explicit error. Optional
model execution was checked on Linux ARM/Python 3.12; core portability checks do
not establish optional spaCy model compatibility on every supported platform.

#### Additional language construction checks

The manually labeled synthetic cases in `tests/fixtures/multilingual_verb_groups.json`
check whole finite-group **tense sequences**, separately from the German
**tense-plus-mood** score above. These are development regression cases, not
independent or representative literary evaluation sets:

| Language / selected model | Matching tense sequences |
| --- | --- |
| English / spaCy medium 3.8.0 | 13 / 14 |
| French / Stanza GSD nocharlm 1.15.0 | 14 / 15 |
| Spanish / spaCy medium 3.8.0 | 14 / 14 |
| Italian / Stanza MarkIT nocharlm 1.15.0 | 17 / 17 |
| Portuguese / spaCy medium 3.8.0 | 15 / 16 |
| Dutch / spaCy medium 3.8.0 | 15 / 15 |

The English model misses a coordinated predicate, French treats `partie` as a
noun in an anterior-perfect example, and Portuguese mistakes synthetic
pluperfect `escrevera` for present. The French spaCy medium baseline matched
10/15 on the same cases, including future/conditional mistakes, motivating the
explicit Stanza option. No model is declared universally best. English/Dutch
missing Mood stays `unmarked`; conditionals and modal forms are separate, not
ordinary past. Unknown morphology, ambiguous `zijn` state/perfect-passive
readings and incompatible finite carriers stay unresolved. Analytic prospective
constructions and indirect/free indirect discourse are not comprehensively
classified. A matching tense sequence does not validate mood, voice, aspect,
quotation interpretation or warning usefulness.

#### Official scientific corpus feature checks

[Universal Dependencies 2.18](https://universaldependencies.org/) (15 May 2026)
provides the official token-annotation reference. The first 100 sentences in file
order from each tagged test partition were checked locally, 700 total. Selected
models parsed all 700 after unknown word morphology was retained explicitly.
This is a bounded **token-feature agreement** check, not a compound verb-group
tense benchmark or a representative accuracy estimate:

| Treebank, r2.18 test | Indicative token Tense matches / eligible |
| --- | --- |
| [German HDT](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/de_hdt/index.html) | 49 / 55 |
| [English EWT](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/en_ewt/index.html) | 141 / 169 |
| [French GSD](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/fr_gsd/index.html), selected Stanza | 149 / 149 |
| [Spanish AnCora](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/es_ancora/index.html) | 195 / 201 |
| [Italian MarkIT](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/it_markit/index.html) | 265 / 269 |
| [Portuguese Bosque](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/pt_bosque/index.html) | 109 / 111 |
| [Dutch Alpino](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/nl_alpino/index.html) | 154 / 162 |

Eligible gold features enter the denominator before prediction/alignment checks.
English had 28 eligible finite-word alignment misses; Portuguese had two.
English omitted Mood for 90 aligned eligible words and Dutch for all 162.
Missing gold features are reported separately; they are not invented as gold
labels. Many-to-many expanded word spans are not guessed. HDT has converted
manual morphology; GSD German features have different annotation provenance.
MarkIT includes partially corrected automatic morphology. Training overlap,
annotation conversion, domains and the small ordered prefixes limit interpretation.
Raw external corpus bytes are not bundled; reproducible tools accept explicit
local files and report their SHA256 and caller-supplied provenance:

```sh
python scripts/check_linguistic_corpus.py --conllu de_hdt-ud-test.conllu --language de --model de_core_news_md --limit 100 --corpus UD_German-HDT --release 2.18 --license "CC BY-SA4.0" --source https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UniversalDependencies/UD_German-HDT/r2.18/de_hdt-ud-test.conllu
```

#### Finite-verb detection, separately from feature agreement

The evaluator additionally reports `finite_verb_detection` over **all uniquely
aligned gold words**, including nonverbs. A positive requires `VERB` or `AUX`
and `VerbForm=Fin`. This exposes false-positive finite verbs on gold adjectives
or nouns that the gold-verb-conditioned feature table above cannot measure.
The [CoNLL-U format](https://universaldependencies.org/format.html) distinguishes
syntactic words, surface tokens and morphology; expanded many-to-many spans
remain unscored rather than being guessed into alignment.

The independent 28 October 2026 rerun used the same official r2.18 test files,
first 100 sentences per language and local model versions listed above. French
was rerun with both the earlier spaCy medium baseline and selected Stanza GSD.
All original feature metrics, including eligible Tense denominators, matched
the retained previous reports exactly. No sentence failed source reconstruction
or parsing in these eight runs. Counts below are **conditional on unique exact
alignment**, not end-to-end detection across excluded words:

| Test partition / parser | Aligned / all gold words | TP / FP / FN | Precision / recall |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| German HDT / spaCy md | 1656 / 1700 | 119 / 5 / 4 | 0.960 / 0.967 |
| English EWT / spaCy md | 2110 / 2202 | 166 / 4 / 12 | 0.976 / 0.933 |
| French GSD / spaCy md baseline | 2395 / 2584 | 149 / 1 / 9 | 0.993 / 0.943 |
| Spanish AnCora / spaCy md | 2944 / 3076 | 220 / 2 / 2 | 0.991 / 0.991 |
| Italian MarkIT / Stanza | 2868 / 3224 | 292 / 2 / 4 | 0.993 / 0.986 |
| Portuguese Bosque / spaCy md | 1563 / 1797 | 128 / 0 / 0 | 1.000 / 1.000 |
| Dutch Alpino / spaCy md | 2049 / 2049 | 157 / 5 / 5 | 0.969 / 0.969 |
| French GSD / Stanza | 2414 / 2584 | 158 / 0 / 0 | 1.000 / 1.000 |

The JSON separately reports gold/predicted alignment misses and unscored words
from source/parse failures. A gold verb without unambiguous finiteness is not
invented as a negative: one aligned French word per run and one Portuguese word
were excluded from detection labels. Missing predicted verb finiteness is
counted explicitly; it misses a known gold finite verb rather than manufacturing
a resolved prediction. Undefined precision/recall denominators produce `null`.
Italian MarkIT, Portuguese and French Stanza each had one aligned prediction
without verb finiteness in this bounded rerun.

These are token-detection and token-feature checks. They do not validate composed
verb-group tense, narration attribution, editorial warnings or literary quality.
The ordered sample, alignment exclusions, corpus annotation provenance and
possible training overlap prevent representative accuracy or a general parser
ranking. In particular, perfect scores on the selected aligned subset do not
establish perfect detection in excluded spans or unseen literary text.

### Core validation status

**Since v0.7.6:** seven short original-language literary excerpts have manually
transcribed sentence boundaries and orthographic tokens in
[`tests/fixtures/literary_reference.json`](https://github.com/mfahsold/lixity/blob/main/tests/fixtures/literary_reference.json).
They cover 375 tokens and 14 sentences, with edition URLs, extraction locators
and public-domain provenance. The same expectations check corpus, chapter and
paragraph counts and the real CLI. Native browser checks compare displayed
sentence counts, paragraph means, localized units and exact highlights with the
same annotations in all seven languages, NFC/NFD spellings and desktop/mobile.
The expected tokens are not generated by the engine.

| Measurement | Evidence so far | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Words and sentences | Manual literary boundaries/tokens agree across backend, CLI and UI on the reference excerpts. | Representative per-language segmentation accuracy. |
| Unicode and literal evidence | Canonical-equivalent counting, original hashes/offsets and complete-cluster mappings have positive and negative fixtures. | Full grapheme-aware tokenization or guessed mappings across excluded Markdown regions. |
| Nominal, passive and other lexical cues | Controlled positive/negative examples check listed patterns, agreement variants and overrides. | Contextual part-of-speech, voice, tense or nominal-style classification. |
| Syllables and readability | Selected dictionary divisions and named coefficient arithmetic are checked. | Language-wide pronunciation accuracy, comprehension or novel-quality prediction. |
| Statistical comparisons | Controlled formula/edge cases check robust spread, adjusted deviations, lexical estimators and rank-space computations. | Calibrated chapter p-values, independent sentences or genre-wide inference. |
| Presentation | Real localized values, units, source ranges, scope distinctions and mobile visibility are exercised. | A measured author/editor comprehension or usability-study result. |

The works are Fontane's *Effi Briest*, Austen's *Pride and Prejudice*, Flaubert's
*Madame Bovary*, Cervantes's *Don Quijote*, Collodi's *Pinocchio*, Queirós's
*Os Maias* and Multatuli's *Max Havelaar*. Per-excerpt counts and provenance
remain in the reference fixture, rather than being duplicated here.

These are regression examples, not a representative literary corpus or a
held-out evaluation of grammar, syllables, readability or literary quality.
Historical spelling and deliberately short selections limit generalization.
Passing them establishes the stated counting conventions on those passages.

Reference units must agree before comparing systems. Lixity's orthographic
tokens differ from UD's syntactic words: contractions and clitics can be one
written token but several syntactic words. An annotated-corpus evaluation must
reconstruct the surface tokens and compare character boundaries, rather than
label every token-total difference a bug. See the
[UD evaluation protocol](https://universaldependencies.org/conll18/evaluation.html)
and [tokenization conventions](https://universaldependencies.org/u/overview/tokenization.html).
Similarly, [UD tense features](https://universaldependencies.org/u/feat/Tense.html)
describe words, which need not have the tense of an entire compound construction.

External sentence-boundary audits must record the treebank release, test
partition, source/license hashes, sample rule and reconstruction protocol.
Exact sentence-end precision/recall can be measured against UD `# text` units
without treating syntactic word counts as orthographic gold. Joining units into
artificial paragraphs tests boundary stress cases, but loses natural paragraph
context: unpunctuated headings and colon-separated units can then appear as
missed boundaries. Such scores describe agreement under that protocol, not
language-wide or novel-specific accuracy. Exclude forced batch-final boundaries
from scoring and keep undefined rates unknown rather than reporting zero.

Bounded corrections have separate positive and negative fixtures: regular
plural passive participles in Spanish, Italian and Portuguese, French
`fut`/`furent`, nominal ending number variants and German `zur`. The
[Italian](https://universaldependencies.org/it/dep/aux-pass.html) and
[French](https://universaldependencies.org/fr/dep/aux-pass.html) UD examples
provide grammatical references, not measured precision/recall for these regexes.
Portuguese marked hiatus is checked against dictionary syllabifications such as
[saída](https://dicionario.priberam.org/sa%C3%ADda) and
[saúde](https://dicionario.priberam.org/sa%C3%BAde); Dutch trema boundaries follow
[official language advice](https://www.vlaanderen.be/team-taaladvies/taaladviezen/idee-ideeen-ideeen-ideen).
Dutch `ij` is counted separately from adjacent vowels, following dictionary
divisions such as [bij.en](https://anw.ivdnt.org/article/bij) and
[bij.een](https://anw.ivdnt.org/article/bijeen). Paired closing quotation marks
separated from terminal punctuation by spaces remain in their original sentence;
negative fixtures distinguish a following opening quote and blank-line boundaries.
Their effects reach syllables-per-word and the declared readability formula.

The Italian counter was compared post hoc against the `word` and `SumSylls`
fields in [PhonItalia 1.10](https://github.com/stefanocoretta/phonItaliaR/tree/main/data-raw/phonItalia-1.10)
(source TSV SHA-256 `22d22409c1fc3ad2844f47543f3017c50ef9d3f95f5196093ff2203d7f071b17`).
Run `PYTHONPATH=src python scripts/evaluate_phonitalia.py PATH_TO_WORDFORMS_TSV`
to reproduce aggregate agreement without copying the lexicon into Lixity.
Of 120,000 rows, 4,170 were excluded by the alphabetic-word/positive-count
filter; 90,134 of 115,830 remaining rows agreed exactly (77.82%), with mean
absolute difference 0.230 syllables. The sample contains 90,681 distinct
spellings, so repeated forms retain row weight. These are lexicon agreements,
not a language-wide accuracy estimate: pronunciation, dialect, token frequency,
syllabification conventions and literary usage vary. No separate literary
holdout or human listening evaluation was used.

The same command also compares the production estimator with an **experimental,
unshipped** rising-diphthong rule. It groups case-normalized NFC spellings,
excludes the 16 spellings with differing source counts and partitions the 90,665
remaining word types by SHA-256 modulo five. On the 18,156-type comparison
partition, exact agreement rises from 13,944 to 17,248 and mean absolute
difference falls from 0.2405 to 0.0505; nevertheless, 469 forms become worse
while 3,771 improve. This partition was inspected during development and is
not an untouched holdout; these figures do not measure performance on novels
or token-weighted text. The candidate incorrectly merges common hiatuses such
as `io` and `mio`, because unmarked stress cannot reliably be inferred from the
letters alone. It was therefore not enabled. Italian phonology distinguishes
[rising diphthongs](https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/dittongo_%28Enciclopedia-dell%27Italiano%29/)
from [hiatuses](https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/iato_%28Enciclopedia-dell%27Italiano%29/);
pronunciation varies with lexical and linguistic context. A larger independent
literary evaluation and a suitable stress-aware pronunciation resource remain
necessary before changing this counter.

For French, `PYTHONPATH=src python scripts/evaluate_lexique.py PATH_TO_TSV`
compares an experimental removal of the final `-ent` deduction with the
`1_Mot` and `26_SyllNb` fields of [Lexique 4.10](https://www.lexique.org/databases/Lexique410/Lexique4.1.zip)
(New et al., 2026; CC BY-SA 4.0; extracted TSV SHA-256
`f112ad487334c8ab702e6b95cf08110b2ac534d1896e1643f9c669f91a139a84`).
Among 12,705 unique alphabetic `-ent` spellings with one agreed count, 7,011
improve but 5,594 become worse; 26 ambiguous spellings are excluded. This is
type-weighted agreement with the lexicon, not accuracy on literary text. Its
syllable counts are algorithmically derived from phonological forms with final
schwas removed; real speakers can pronounce those schwas in some contexts.
The French counter remains unchanged: distinguishing spoken endings from
silent verb inflections requires additional contextual evidence.

The audit also reproduces unresolved weaknesses:

| Area | Observed limitation and interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| Unicode | NFC equivalence is corrected, preserving source bytes and offsets. Combining sequences without a precomposed letter can still exceed the word patterns' coverage; the mapper does not claim full grapheme segmentation. See [Unicode UAX #29](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr29/). |
| Tense | Curated present-only forms no longer also count as productive past candidates. Listed German perfect/pluperfect pairs count as one construction across chapter, scene and paragraph analysis, with bounded intervening words. Unlicensed auxiliary/participle combinations retain both cues; regional/transitive variants, unlisted forms and other languages can still produce spurious mixed classifications. A `mixed` result is not proof of a grammatical tense switch. English `read` and Portuguese `falamos` require context. |
| Spanish compound cues | Under the default lexical patterns, adjacent present-tense `haber` plus a detected regular `-ado/-ido` candidate is counted once as past, not again as present. This remains a surface pattern: irregular participles and intervening adverbs may be missed, and the broad past bucket does not establish the construction's temporal reference. French, Italian and Dutch compound cues may still count auxiliary and participle in both categories. Custom patterns and optional contextual models are unchanged. |
| Dialogue | Romance language profiles (`fr`, `es`, `it`, `pt`) recognize line-initial dialogue dashes (`^[—–]`), but inline mid-paragraph dashes and unclosed quotes remain outside default patterns. Zero detected quotation words does not establish absence of speech. Overlapping custom matches can count the same words in more than one turn. Counts and shares of quoted words use the union of recognized ranges. |
| Syllables | Italian `count_it()` strips silent `qu`/`gu` and merges rising `[iu]`+vowel diphthongs; unmarked hiatuses (`paura`, `mio` vs. `fiore`) and stress-dependent splits remain heuristic. French `count_fr()` adds exceptions for `-ment` mute verbs, `souvent`, and `-éC+ent`, while remaining orthographic rather than phonological. The corrected Dutch `ij` rule is not a complete pronunciation model. Generic `count_generic()` retains only ASCII `a–z` letters (`[aeiouy]+` nuclei); non-Latin tokens yield zero syllables (causing Flesch/ASW to report unavailable when `asw == 0.0` while LIX remains measured), and non-ASCII Latin diacritics outside the seven language profiles are stripped. |
| Sentence spans | Sentence-final abbreviations can merge sentences. Paired spaced closers and German single `‚…‘` closers have direct boundary/evidence controls, but quotation pairing and abbreviation tables are incomplete; a matching total does not guarantee correct boundaries. |
| Nominal/passive cues | Word endings and auxiliary patterns do not resolve lexical category, adjectival participles or syntactic voice. Short regular and selected irregular passive forms have positive/negative controls; German `ist geöffnet` state passive remains outside the event-passive cue pattern. Coverage is improved, not complete. |

Readability research evaluates defined tasks and datasets, often combining
lexical, syntactic and discourse features. It does not make a syllable/length
formula a comprehension test for these novels; see
[Lee et al. (2021)](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.834/).
Future corpus evaluation must report per-language boundary precision/recall,
cue precision/recall against appropriate annotations and the dataset/genre;
arithmetic tests, UI localization and highlighted count agreement are separate
checks. No novel-wide accuracy percentage is claimed here.

Potential external references include [Corpus REDEWIEDERGABE](https://aclanthology.org/2020.lrec-1.100/),
whose historical German material distinguishes direct, indirect and other
speech or thought representation, and [GermAnProse](https://aclanthology.org/2026.latechclfl-1.25/),
which provides narrative annotations for four German short prose texts. Neither
is a representative contemporary multilingual benchmark; annotation schemes,
text editions, permitted uses and span/token conventions must be checked before
comparison. GermAnProse has not been evaluated in this project.

An exploratory comparison against the fictional subset of the
[REDEWIEDERGABE consensus corpus](https://github.com/redewiedergabe/corpus)
(commit `45abfcf5f9c2a3d9a903f5c68f8f5b36bbce5563`, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
can be reproduced with `PYTHONPATH=src python scripts/evaluate_redewiedergabe.py
PATH_TO_DATA_MAIN_XML`. The script retains and outputs only aggregate counts;
the corpus remains a separately supplied resource. It flattens the TEI body,
preserving Unicode codepoint offsets and nested spans, and compares the German
production quotation and word regexes with `direct`/`speech` annotations at
word-token level. Mixed-medium, borderline direct spans and tokens crossing
annotation or match boundaries are excluded. This matches the exact patterns,
not the full Markdown manuscript preprocessing pipeline.

For 395 fictional samples (aggregate source SHA-256
`4cd63654a362794be47effe6856ac1526660fbd13a6a31c817c4c95266c9fd3f`),
the comparison has 39,455 true positives, 1,681 positive disagreements,
17,501 negative disagreements and 143,202 true negatives; 527 ambiguous and
zero boundary-crossing tokens were excluded. The resulting token precision is
95.9% and recall 69.3%. These are disagreements between quotation-mark cues
and direct-speech annotations: quoted thoughts or writing may be positive
disagreements even when the quotation cue is correct. Excerpt boundaries,
historical conventions, tokenization and annotation scope matter, and the
inspected corpus is not a held-out or representative contemporary evaluation.

#### Synthetic held-out contemporary-style prose benchmark (EN & DE)

To evaluate default heuristics on contemporary-style literary prose (distinct
from the 19th-century public-domain excerpts and development fixtures),
`PYTHONPATH=src python scripts/evaluate_contemporary_prose.py` (with optional
`--json`) runs an offline, deterministic, stdlib-only benchmark over freshly
authored English and German passages covering sentence boundaries (abbreviations
such as `Dr.`, `z. B.`, `Dept.`, `Tel.`, ellipses, dialogue punctuation,
staccato sentences, numbers/initials), dialogue cues (standard quotation marks,
non-speech quotes such as signs/scare quotes, dash-introduced speech, unquoted
interior thoughts, and free indirect speech), and finite tense cues (past,
present, compound perfect, mixed narration/dialogue, and lexically ambiguous
verbs). Internal sentence boundaries exclude forced passage-final ends.

| Language | Task | Sample | TP / FP / FN | Precision (95% Wilson CI) | Recall (95% Wilson CI) | F1 |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- | --- | ---: |
| EN | Sentence boundaries | 15 passages / 39 sents / 24 bounds | 22 / 1 / 2 | 95.7% [79.0%, 99.2%] | 91.7% [74.2%, 97.7%] | 93.6% |
| EN | Dialogue cues (all) | 16 passages / 217 tokens | 49 / 5 / 77 | 90.7% [80.1%, 96.0%] | 38.9% [30.8%, 47.6%] | 54.4% |
| EN | Tense cues (combined) | 32 passages / 64 cues | 48 / 4 / 16 | 92.3% [81.8%, 97.0%] | 75.0% [63.2%, 84.0%] | 82.8% |
| EN | Tense cues (past) | 39 gold cues | 36 / 2 / 3 | 94.7% [82.7%, 98.5%] | 92.3% [79.7%, 97.3%] | 93.5% |
| EN | Tense cues (present) | 25 gold cues | 12 / 2 / 13 | 85.7% [60.1%, 96.0%] | 48.0% [30.0%, 66.5%] | 61.5% |
| DE | Sentence boundaries | 15 passages / 40 sents / 25 bounds | 23 / 1 / 2 | 95.8% [79.8%, 99.3%] | 92.0% [75.0%, 97.8%] | 93.9% |
| DE | Dialogue cues (all) | 16 passages / 199 tokens | 44 / 3 / 71 | 93.6% [82.8%, 97.8%] | 38.3% [29.9%, 47.4%] | 54.3% |
| DE | Tense cues (combined) | 32 passages / 61 cues | 35 / 5 / 26 | 87.5% [73.9%, 94.5%] | 57.4% [44.9%, 69.0%] | 69.3% |
| DE | Tense cues (past) | 34 gold cues | 22 / 1 / 12 | 95.7% [79.0%, 99.2%] | 64.7% [47.9%, 78.5%] | 77.2% |
| DE | Tense cues (present) | 27 gold cues | 13 / 4 / 14 | 76.5% [52.7%, 90.4%] | 48.1% [30.7%, 66.0%] | 59.1% |

Dialogue breakdown by category shows why aggregate dialogue recall is low on
contemporary prose: on `standard_quoted` passages, default quotation scanning
achieves 100.0% precision and recall (EN: 49/49, 95% Wilson CI [92.7%, 100.0%];
DE: 44/44, [92.0%, 100.0%]), while `non_speech_quote` (signs and scare quotes)
produces false positives (EN: 5 FP; DE: 3 FP), and contemporary unmarked forms
all record 0.0% recall under default EN/DE rules (`dash_speech` EN 0/19
[0.0%, 16.8%], DE 0/23 [0.0%, 14.3%]; `interior_thought` EN 0/22 [0.0%, 14.9%],
DE 0/17 [0.0%, 18.4%]; `free_indirect` EN 0/36 [0.0%, 9.6%], DE 0/31
[0.0%, 11.0%]). Sentence-boundary misses come from unlisted abbreviations
(`Dept.`, `Tel.`), sentence-final protected abbreviations (`Ltd.`, `usw.`), and
sentence-ending Unicode ellipses (`…`). Tense-cue misses reflect Lixity's
incomplete default lexicons (no productive present-tense rule in either
language, and German's v0.7.7 removal of the unrestricted `-te/-ten` suffix
rule so unlisted regular preterites are missed) plus ambiguous verb forms.

**Explicit limitations:** this benchmark is a small, synthetic, author-constructed
held-out set, not a representative sample of published contemporary fiction.
The wide 95% Wilson intervals reflect small sample sizes, dialogue recall
depends directly on the chosen proportion of quoted vs. unmarked speech and
thought, and only the default offline heuristic path (without optional
spaCy/Stanza models) is evaluated here.

### Voice-reference diagnostics limits

`audio-reference inspect` measures level, noise floor, clipping and spectral
bandwidth of a saved reference. Its notes use fixed engineering thresholds
without corpus calibration. Listen to the reference and a rendered passage to
assess suitability, including transcript accuracy, accent and resemblance to
the speaker. These qualities are outside the diagnostic's measurements.
A prior local OpenVoice V2 check used one target reference and one converter.
The render retained content up to about 11 kHz with a wideband reference and
lost content above about 8 kHz with a reference lacking those frequencies.
See the [voice-reference methods](METHODS.md#12-voice-reference-signal-diagnostics-audio-reference-inspect).

<a id="chapter-audio-comparison-limits-unreleased"></a>
<a id="chapter-audio-comparison-limits"></a>

### Chapter audio comparison limits

`audio-inspect` and `audio-verify` add local chapter-level observations and
optional plan/transcript comparison; [METHODS](METHODS.md#13-chapter-audio-audit-unreleased)
defines their formulas. Synthetic fixtures test PCM arithmetic, stereo handling,
silence boundaries, malformed input and transcript identity. They do not establish
perceptual quality, natural rhythm, recognition accuracy or speaker consistency.
Full-scale samples indicate possible clipping, not proven audible distortion.
The 20 ms/−50 dBFS/0.1 second silence rule is uncalibrated: quiet speech can fall
below it, and breath or room noise can remain above it. Bandwidth and noise floor
are explicitly unknown for this audit. Zero-amplitude dBFS is negative infinity,
represented as null, not a finite noise-floor estimate.

The audit takes supplied word timestamps as evidence. They may come from manual
annotation or a separate recognizer, including the optional `audio-transcribe`
workflow. The SHA-256 binding checks file identity. Transcript correctness and
timing accuracy still depend on how the evidence was produced.
Comparison misses may be recognizer errors, tokenization differences or actual
speech differences. Coverage is alignment coverage, not an accuracy probability.
Repeated wording can create alternative alignments. Missing expected words have
no known timestamp; neighboring timestamps only bracket a possible location.
Pause differences are available only at fully aligned boundaries and use external
word timing. A time gap may contain breath or noise. Absence of a discrepancy is
not proof that every spoken word or pause matches the plan. Missing transcript,
unanchored boundaries and exhausted measurement scope remain unknown.

### Speech control evidence

Pronunciation and delivery support describe the inputs an adapter can take.
A respelling changes the text passed to the model. An IPA-capable adapter routes
the author's validated phone sequence into the model. Structured prosody routes
numeric controls into the acoustic model. Listen for the target pronunciation,
prosody and continuity of the author's voice in the rendered passage. A valid
sequence or a successful request leaves those outcomes unmeasured.

External synthesis uses an explicitly configured provider. The operator declares
whether its adapter accepts free-text delivery instructions. How a model follows
them depends on the runtime, checkpoint, language and passage. JSON retains the
authored instructions. SSML projects the controls it can represent and warns
when a control needs a separate handoff. A receiving engine may interpret voice,
rate and delivery differently. Local analysis and audio inspection stay local.

Explicit pauses and edge fades can be verified at the PCM sample level. The
pause audible between words also depends on synthesized silence and breath.
The taper smooths the waveform at a join over a short fixed window. It has no
perceptual calibration or validation for long-form speaker consistency. Browser
and synthetic fixture checks verify operation and contract behavior. They supply
no blinded listening evidence about model or recording quality.
See the [pronunciation, delivery and PCM methods](METHODS.md#143-pronunciation-and-delivery-planning).

### Continuous Flow-Matching diffusion synthesis limits (`f5-tts`)

The current bundled F5 loader is unavailable. Existing profiles and retained
artifacts remain readable; transport, cache or export support does not establish
a working local inference runtime. Do not select an F5 profile expecting model
installation or a worker switch. See [retained F5 profiles](AUDIO.md#retained-f5-tts-profiles-unreleased)
for the explicit external-worker boundary and current alternatives.

No model architecture guarantees repetition-free, intelligible or speaker-matched
output. A compatible external runtime, its checkpoint and reference recording
need their own listening and resource checks; previous synthesis descriptions
are not validation of a currently installed runtime.

### Manual manuscript association limits

Manually selected quotes require explicit retention and exact source/paragraph/claim
pins. Anchor review detects structural changes, not semantic contradictions or
factual support. Moved or ambiguous quotes require review; claim pins change only
through an explicit revision. Zero saved links do not prove a claim is unused.
The source recheck is optimistic and does not lock manuscript editors. Backups
include retained private quotes; this workflow creates no full manuscript blob.
See [retention and compatibility](research/USAGE.md#associate-a-manuscript-quote-with-a-claim).

### Research and external-library limits

Zotero owns bibliography and reading; Lixity retains selected evidence and authored
records. Their backup requirements are separate. An integrity audit verifies
retained bytes, references and citations; it cannot verify historical truth,
chronology or the completeness of an external library. Native integration checks
are bounded synthetic tests, not certification of every platform or collection.

Source analysis uses its own `source_internal` reference and unverified supplied
context. Retaining a historical source does not make it a manuscript style norm;
lexical overlap does not establish factual support or appropriate context.
Search does not resolve contradictory prose or accept a hypothesis for the author.

PNG/JPEG images retain exact source versions and stay outside text analysis.
Header validation and browser preview do not establish complete codec validity or
historical authenticity. Geographic coordinates and routes are authored data;
rendering a map does not verify a journey or sightline. An unavailable image
never silently resolves to a different version.

RIS migration is additive; verify attachment identities, retained citations and
restoration before retiring a workflow. Automatic background/cloud synchronization,
audio/video transcription, image OCR and visual AI are not implemented. PDF
extraction or an external OCR worker does not establish recognition accuracy.
Current media, provider and schema boundaries live in [Research usage](research/USAGE.md).

### Robust comparisons and statistical claims

Median/MAD and the noise-adjusted $z^*$ describe contrast within the supplied
manuscript. A normal-consistency multiplier does not make arbitrary chapter
features normally distributed; `split_mad()`, `medcouple()`, `adjusted_boxplot_fences()`,
and `huber_location()` expose skew-aware and M-estimator primitives without
replacing the chapter-baseline assumptions. When `MAD = 0` on a varying series,
`StyleFingerprint` falls back to `sn_estimator()` / `qn_estimator()`, marking
`zero_mad_varying` only if both are non-positive or non-finite. Jeffreys
continuity-adjusted binomial/Poisson SEs and the sample-SD `asl` SE prevent
zero-SE collapse on 0%/100% or zero-hit chapters without establishing population
certainty; missing SE still means no estimated measurement error.

BH/BY are established selection procedures **given valid null probabilities**
and their dependence conditions. Lixity's normal-tail probabilities suffer from
**self-calibration circularity**: each chapter contributes to the manuscript's
own median and MAD against which it is then scored, inducing in-sample
dependence and finite-sample ratio distortions whose null calibration is not
established. Applying BH or BY to these same-manuscript scores—or inspecting
exploratory runs/lag diagnostics—does not repair that circularity.
`fdr_flagged` is therefore an **uncalibrated descriptive selection** under the
implemented model, and `expected_false_positives` is a standard-normal reference
expectation, not an observed error count. Establishing calibrated inferential
thresholds remains an open boundary for future work (for example, via
leave-one-out chapter baselines or constrained block/chapter-order permutation
tests under explicit exchangeability strata; naive chapter-label permutation
alone preserves unordered values and cannot calibrate same-sample outlier
scores). Cliff's delta describes ordinal contrast, not quality.
Definitions and active thresholds: [METHODS §§1–4](METHODS.md#1-robust-house-style-baseline).

The additive `meta.interpretation` legend identifies model selection explicitly.
With two distinct observations per feature, z* is available but its ideal
exact-arithmetic magnitude is bounded by 1/1.4826. The default cutoff cannot
flag ordinary such pairs; numerical midpoint rounding can exceed the ideal
bound. Per-feature zero-SE bounds guard unreachable-cutoff claims and a
rounding-sensitive status discloses material differences. The UI/text
warn per feature about unreachable cutoffs. Neither five observations nor any
other fixed minimum establishes inferential validity; no general n≥3 MAD ceiling
is assumed. Paragraph marks, chapter bands, deviation flags and FDR have different
reference populations/rules and must not be treated as one decision threshold.

Paragraph comparisons use a chapter-local reference. Short paragraphs, fewer
than three eligible paragraphs or a zero scale can leave the comparison
unknown even when the value is measured. Many zero pattern counts can yield
a zero scale even after the Sn and Qn fallbacks.
Measured values remain available for passage review.
[Paragraph comparison method](METHODS.md#9-paragraph-layers-within-chapter-colouring)

Style axes now use PCA of standardized tied midranks on one common complete
chapter set, with ridge shrinkage $(1-\lambda)C + \lambda I$ when $n \le p$ or
$\lambda_{\min} \le 10^{-6}\lambda_{\max}$ and regularized Mahalanobis distances
($D_M$) per complete chapter. **Since v0.9.1:** the distance uses the same
standardized midrank rows as the covariance. Earlier builds could instead use
noise-adjusted z* cells, yielding an incoherent distance; historical values must
be recomputed. Synthetic tests check a closed-form collinear solution, the
production `from_metrics()` path, ties, incomplete chapters and invariance to
optional z* fields. These establish coordinate correctness, not calibration.
The reported eigenvalue shares belong to the regularized matrix and need not
match empirical score-variance shares. Covariance and scores share the rank space;
missing measurements are not imputed. At least three complete chapters and
three varying baseline-usable features are required, with constant columns
dropped on that set. Incomplete chapters have no dimension scores. Complete-case selection, small samples, and shrinkage regularization still limit interpretation. Score flags and Mahalanobis distances are
descriptive and do not validate prose quality or simultaneous confidence.
See [METHODS §5](METHODS.md#5-exploratory-style-dimensions).

### Lexical diversity

Length, local vocabulary and estimator parameters affect different indices.
[Bestgen (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12630) studies English learner essays
and monologues; 60 tokens is one truncation condition, not a universal floor.
Its main experiment uses a 50-token draw/window parameter, so it does not
directly calibrate Lixity's 42-token HD-D.
[Kyle et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263123000402) assesses optimized
oral-task variants, not Lixity's defaults on German novels. Neither establishes
genre-wide reliability for the local 100-token policy. Guiraud remains sensitive
to length; fixed-window MATTR and fixed-draw HD-D still depend on their parameters
and the supplied vocabulary distribution.

HD-D is exact expected TTR for a fixed draw. Exact computation removes Monte Carlo
error, not population uncertainty. MTLD enforces `DEFAULT_MTLD_MIN_FACTOR_LEN = 5`
so short initial repetitions do not complete premature factors, and `yules_k()`
uses the finite-sample $N(N-1)$ denominator (`0.0` for $N \le 1$ or all-unique
tokens). MTLD variants also differ in direction
averaging, threshold and trailing-factor rules. Compare measurements only after
aligning formulas, parameters and segmentation; regenerate historical reports
when those contracts changed. See [formula and guard details](METHODS.md#6-lexical-diversity-indices).

### Linguistic proxies and literary interpretation

Analysis shares a bounded Markdown prose projection. Link labels contribute;
destinations, images, code, comments and excluded document regions do not.
Paragraph profiles preserve displayed text and source anchors separately from
counting. The configured token rules and narrower paragraph scope do not imply
complete CommonMark support or linguistic token accuracy. See
[analysis scope](METHODS.md) for the unit and denominator of each measurement.

Passive, tense, adjective, nominalization and modality fields count lexical
markers or suffixes. For example, German `werden` also marks future tense or
becoming; English `been` also appears in active perfect constructions. These
counts do not identify syntactic voice or distinguish epistemic uncertainty
from obligation. Sentence segmentation and syllables are also heuristic;
utterance abbreviations (`no.`, `co.`) split sentences and tokenless
fragments do not count as sentences.
Suffix cues over-include on purpose-ambiguous words: English nominal `-th`
counts *month/health/truth*, German adjective `-ig`/`-al` count
*König/Saal*, German nominal `-ik`/`-ur` count *Musik/Natur*. Modal lexicons
have unequal morphology coverage (German and Dutch include preterite forms,
the other five language profiles cover present forms only, and `generic` has no
modal lexicon), so `modal_density` is **not comparable across languages**.

In `generic` mode, `count_generic()` strips all characters outside ASCII `a–z`
before counting `[aeiouy]+` vowel nuclei. Non-Latin scripts (such as Cyrillic,
Greek, Arabic, or CJK) therefore yield zero estimated syllables (`asw == 0.0`,
causing syllable-based readability to report unavailable while LIX remains
measured), and non-ASCII Latin diacritics outside the seven named language
profiles are silently stripped from syllable estimation.

Readability coefficient tests verify the declared formulas, not their original
calibration or reader comprehension. Amstad's original coefficient page and
calibration protocol have not been verified here. The seven named formulas use
distinct intercepts and ASL/ASW weights calibrated under different language
conventions: scores may fall outside 0–100 and are **not comparable across
languages or translations**. The dashboard shows the inputs
beside the heuristic results, including the estimated status of syllable counts.
[German PALME research
(2026)](https://aclanthology.org/2026.bea-1.6/) separates controlled detector tests
from graded-reader evaluation; its results do not validate Lixity's regex cues.

Showing/telling is a composite of those visible signals. Empty rankings and
zero fallback scores do not establish equal artistic effect. Without explicit
dividers, pacing scenes are chapter placeholders. Short sentences, perception
verbs and vocabulary contrast do not establish immersion, tension or a reason
to rewrite. Repeated sentence-start runs (`repeated_start_runs`) do not
distinguish rhetorical anaphora from unintentional repetition, and adjacent
sentence content-word overlap (`sentence_overlap_pct`) measures exact
lowercased surface-token sharing within paragraphs rather than semantic
coherence, coreference or inflected lemmas. Similarly, dialogue cadence
(`short_turns`, `long_turns`) and quoted-versus-narration sentence length
contrast (`dialogue_asl`, `narration_asl`, `asl_contrast`) operate on
recognized quotation spans rather than speaker turns: a single utterance
interrupted by an unquoted reporting clause counts as two shorter quoted spans
and leaves the reporting clause in unquoted narration. Scene/register targets are explicit author preferences, never
hardcoded genre norms. [Underwood's expert discussion](https://tedunderwood.com/2024/01/05/can-language-models-predict-the-next-twist-in-a-story/)
illustrates why surface predictability and narrative experience differ.

Dialogue turns are quotation segments without speaker attribution. Character
mentions depend on supplied names or literal project aliases; declared viewpoint
chapters are separate metadata, not inferred first-person presence. There is no
NER or coreference. Hook and repetition scores also locate surface patterns;
deliberate calm endings and repeated motifs can be appropriate author choices.

#### Scene evidence and author intent

The scene tracks report recognized quotation-word share and mean words per
sentence in manuscript order. Quotation marks may enclose a letter or a term.
Indirect speech and other unmarked voices can lie outside the recognized
ranges. The block distribution depends on the configured quotation and word
rules and the reported short and long cutoffs. It describes textual length.
The interface shows unresolved quotation ranges and unavailable measurements
as such. A recognized count of zero leaves undetected speech possible. No
fictional duration, speaking time, speaker identity or reader response follows
from these measurements. [Scene method cards](METHODS.md#scene-evidence-and-dramaturgical-rehearsal)

The within-scene comparisons report signed differences between the two halves
in words per sentence and percentage points. The sample floor is a display
guard. It supplies no calibrated uncertainty for the shifts. The wire value
`steady` means the legacy selection cutoffs were not crossed. A zero shift
between means or shares can coexist with substantial variation inside each
half. The measured scope may be a whole chapter when the text has no explicit
scene divisions.

An author intent records a human's question or hypothesis. A changed source
or analysis context calls for reviewing the anchor. It provides no judgement
of the hypothesis. Reordering cards changes the rehearsal only. Lixity's
analysis claims follow the [evidence ladder](LOCALIZATION.md#evidence-levels-for-analysis-claims).

### Structural diagnostics

These diagnostics preserve their declared numerical definitions; an exact
implementation does not validate the underlying model:

- `pelt_changepoints` uses exact unpruned dynamic programming on
  global-SD-standardized series with mBIC-inspired default penalty $3\ln n$: $O(n^2)$
  time and $O(n)$ storage. The retained singleton/zero-variance guard violates
  the PELT pruning premise, so no pruning or linear-time claim is made.
  Anchored variance updates reduce cancellation; exact optimization of this
  guarded objective does not validate its Gaussian model or a narrative break.
  [Killick et al., Theorem 3.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.1438v3).
- Sn uses the original low outer/high inner medians and factor 1.1926. Qn
  preserves its pairwise-distance rank with modern factor 2.21914; neither
  applies finite-sample correction. Normal-consistency factors, finite bias
  corrections and robustness remain distinct. [Original paper](https://wis.kuleuven.be/stat/robust/papers/publications-1993/rousseeuwcroux-alternativestomedianad-jasa-1993.pdf),
  [maintained reference](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/robustbase/robustbase.pdf).
- Early/late Wasserstein integrates the exact empirical-CDF difference;
  merged CDFs also give KS $D$, with $D=0$ returning $p=1$ and stable survival
  evaluation. The same asymptotic probability model remains: ties, short
  samples, serial dependence and fitted distributions are not calibrated by
  this numerical correction. Mann–Kendall `tau` remains tau-a, with a
  tie-corrected approximate normal probability for $S$ (and Hamed–Rao 1998
  autocorrelation variance correction for $n \ge 8$), not tau-b. `trending_features`
  and `shifted_features` apply Benjamini–Hochberg FDR (`q = fdr_q`) across
  tested features, which still depends on the uncalibrated underlying $p$-values.
- The graph exponent follows the approximate discrete estimator in
  [Clauset–Shalizi–Newman Eq. 3.7](https://arxiv.org/abs/0706.1062v2).
  The current continuous fitted CDF and ordinary KS probability do not implement
  its refitted goodness-of-fit procedure. Graph degrees are dependent too;
  neither a fit distance nor a small sample certifies a scale-free graph.

Early/late splits are chapter-count midpoints, not learned narrative boundaries.
Signed Dunning keyness ranks token contrast; it has no multiplicity adjustment.
Chapter-to-rest JSD is raw divergence in nats, not its square-root distance or
an external Delta authorship test. Inspect driver words in context. Formula
details and unchanged field contracts: [METHODS §4c](METHODS.md#4c-structural-diagnostics-structural_diagnostics).

**Accessibility / data visualisation (WCAG 2.2).**
- Colour must never be the only channel (SC 1.4.1, 1.3.3): the heatmap
  prints the numeric z* values, the band chart encodes band/median/outliers
  by position and shape, every chip reveals tense + value as text on click.
